content: For women in the third stage of labor, the use of injectable prostaglandins for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) was evaluated to determine whether it improves maternal and perinatal outcomes compared to placebo or no treatment. If effective, the optimal route of administration and dosing regimen should be identified. Similarly, the use of various uterotonic agents (such as oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol, ergometrine/methylergometrine, injectable prostaglandins, or combinations like oxytocin plus ergometrine or misoprostol plus oxytocin) was compared to other uterotonic agents to assess their safety and efficacy in improving maternal and perinatal outcomes. The goal was to identify the most effective uterotonic agent with the best safety profile, including the appropriate route of administration and dosing regimen. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) initially reviewed each uterotonic option (single agents or combination regimens) against placebo or no uterotonic to evaluate their individual efficacy and safety for PPH prevention. This approach was intended to determine whether each uterotonic could be used independently in settings where other options might not be available. Subsequently, the GDG compared the efficacy and safety of each uterotonic option against others to identify the most effective and safest uterotonic agent, referred to as the uterotonic of choice. The updated World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations on uterotonics for PPH prevention were developed using standardized procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. This process included identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and future updates. Six main groups participated in this process, including the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), WHO Steering Group, Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG), GDG, External Review Group (ERG), and observers from relevant organizations. The GSG, an independent panel of 14 external experts and stakeholders from various WHO regions, identified priority questions and outcomes for the guideline update. The WHO Steering Group, composed of WHO staff, managed the process of updating the recommendations, including evidence retrieval, synthesis, and preparation of the guideline document. The GDG, consisting of 18 external experts and stakeholders with diverse expertise in research, clinical policy, and PPH prevention, appraised and interpreted the evidence to formulate the final recommendations. The ESG, composed of guideline methodologists and systematic review teams, conducted or updated systematic reviews, appraised evidence, and developed evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks. Observers from organizations such as USAID, Jhpiego, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation participated in GDG meetings to provide input on guideline dissemination and implementation. The priority questions for updating the recommendations were identified through a systematic prioritization process, focusing on the anticipated impact of ongoing trials related to PPH prevention. Evidence on the effects of uterotonics was primarily derived from an updated Cochrane systematic review with a network meta-analysis. This review included randomized controlled trials comparing uterotonic agents for PPH prevention in various settings and modes of birth. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, which considers factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency, imprecision, and indirectness. The findings were summarized in Summary of Findings tables, which included effect estimates and quality judgments for each outcome. Additional systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate evidence on values, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. These reviews included studies on women's and healthcare providers' views and experiences, as well as cost-effectiveness analyses of uterotonic agents in different settings. The findings informed the EtD frameworks, which guided the formulation of recommendations. The GDG considered the balance of benefits and harms, resource implications, and contextual factors when formulating recommendations. Uterotonics with clear benefits and minimal harms were more likely to be recommended, while those with uncertain or small net benefits were less likely to be favored.
